summary: Defines a countersignature algorithm for CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE), along with the needed header parameters and CBOR tags. COSE provides security services for CBOR data. It updates RFC 9052. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9338 replaces the earlier COSE countersignature procedure with version 2 forms. The revised signed data includes the cryptographic values needed for the target structure, so a countersignature covers the intended material.

subtitle: A corrected COSE method for adding a second signature to signed, encrypted or MAC-protected data.

tldr.problem: The earlier COSE countersignature description did not always include the computed cryptographic value, so the stated security properties were incorrect for some structures.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9338 defines full and abbreviated version 2 countersignatures and a fixed Countersign_structure that includes the target's relevant cryptographic values.
tldr.outcome: Implementers are encouraged to migrate to the version 2 header parameters, while new implementations must verify the older full countersignature for compatibility. RFC 9338 updates RFC 9052.

facts.label: Tag length for stated collision security

today: RFC 9338 is an Internet Standard (STD 96) published in December 2022. It updates RFC 9052 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Countersignatures Were Revised
sections.content:
Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is designed for small messages and implementations. CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) provides security services for CBOR data. A countersignature is a second signature that confirms a primary signature.

While COSE was advancing to Internet Standard, the security description of the earlier countersignature was found to be incorrect for COSE_Sign1. The earlier algorithm did not always include the cryptographically computed value. RFC 9338 defines a new computation that includes the needed values.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier countersignature process sometimes left out a value needed for the stated security properties. This RFC defines a revised process that includes it.

sections.title: Version 2 Header Parameters
sections.content:
The full version 2 countersignature uses header parameter label 11 and holds one or more COSE_Countersignature values. The abbreviated form uses label 12 and holds a COSE_Countersignature0 value. Both are optional header parameters.

The countersignature parameter may appear as an unprotected attribute in COSE_Sign1, COSE_Signature, COSE_Encrypt, COSE_recipient, COSE_Encrypt0, COSE_Mac and COSE_Mac0 structures defined in RFC 9052.
sections.plainLanguage: COSE has two new header slots for version 2 countersignatures: one for the full form and one for the shorter form. A message can include either slot where the structure permits it.

sections.title: Full and Abbreviated Forms
sections.content:
A full countersignature has the same structure as a COSE signature and can include protected and unprotected attributes. This lets the countersigner identify its key and algorithm, and it allows a countersignature to be countersigned. When tagged, the structure uses CBOR tag 19.

An abbreviated countersignature is a byte string containing only the signature value. It has no protected attributes, so the key and algorithm come from the context used for the related encryption, signature or MAC. The two forms cannot be converted into each other because the structure name is part of the signature computation.
sections.plainLanguage: The full form carries signature metadata as well as the signature. The abbreviated form carries only the signature bytes, and the two forms cannot be substituted for one another.

sections.title: Creating and Verifying a Countersignature
sections.content:
The signer builds a CBOR Countersign_structure from the context name, protected attributes, external additional data, payload and any applicable remaining byte-string fields. The target structure's cryptographic operations must be complete before the countersignature is calculated.

The structure is encoded into the ToBeSigned byte string using the narrowed deterministic CBOR rules. The signing algorithm signs those bytes and the result is stored in the full signature field or abbreviated header attribute. Verification rebuilds and encodes the same structure, checks the signature, and also checks that the key belongs to an authorized identity.
sections.plainLanguage: To create or check a countersignature, both sides build the same ordered data and encode it in the same way. The application must also confirm that the signer is authorized.

sections.title: Registrations and Migration
sections.content:
IANA assigned CBOR tag 19 to COSE_Countersignature. It registered version 2 header parameters with labels 11 and 12 and marked the earlier parameters at labels 7 and 9 as deprecated by RFC 9338.

Implementers are encouraged to move from CounterSignature to CounterSignatureV2 and from CounterSignature0 to CounterSignature0V2. New implementations must support verification of the older full CounterSignature to remain compatible with senders that follow RFC 8152; support for verifying the older abbreviated form is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: New messages should use the version 2 parameters. New implementations still need to verify the older full form so they can accept older messages.

sections.title: Security Limits of Countersigning
sections.content:
Implementations must protect private keys. When more than two parties share an encryption or MAC key, a valid tag does not identify which party created the data, because any key holder can create one.

Short authentication tags on countersigned encrypted or MACed data provide less protection than the same algorithm used with COSE_Sign. To provide 128-bit security against collision attacks, the tag must be at least 256 bits. The RFC gives lower integrity bounds for the cited AES-MAC and AES-CCM cases.
sections.plainLanguage: A countersignature does not identify one creator when several parties share the same key. Short authentication tags also limit the protection the countersignature can provide.
